Senses.Explanation: The twos-and-threes of the Chan records: the scattered knots — the sages themselves split at the cut road-head, the fed assembly straying to the water-side, the way-man's walking with each not knowing the other, and the ferry's boats at rest. Tianyi Yihuai takes up the nine-jointed staff: cut through the road-head of the thousand sages, and Manjushri and Samantabhadra lose their seats in a fright, the ten-stage sages falling outright into twos and threes — then down from the seat, Wuzhun Shifan turns the two wheels: the food-wheel and the way-wheel both turning, the food's strength lasting seven days, then digested — the way forgotten with it — so off you go in twos and threes, by the water and under the trees, calling each other to roam, Guyin Yuncong is asked the way-man's walking and answers: in twos and threes, each not knowing the other; pressed for the bottom of it: tongue-cutting is your share, and Zhe'an Jingfan welcomes the worn travelers: by boat and by land, before and behind, through how many river-bends and mountain-turns, through endless perilous slopes — twos and threes gathering at the Yunmen gate, a rarely-met karmic meeting, gladly taking the rough fist and hot staff, hoping one half of one will thunder once in the layered clouds and heavy fog — not only the black dragon changing bone and the mist-leopard baring its pattern, but the eye of the way seen round and the true wind unfallen. Xingkong Xingzhen opens the third-month third: good things of many kinds — creek peaches spraying fire, bank willows dropping mist, purple swallows warbling deepest truth, partridges calling till the whole mechanism shows — spring light over the fields, spring color joining the sky: in twos and threes seeking the green, in threes and twos heel to heel and shoulder to shoulder, the fisherman casting his line, the herd-boy riding — every head on target, no thing leaning — then three monkeys winnowing coins on the pole-tip, Miyin Zhenchuan takes the meeting of the tenth-direction worlds — all the buddhas' life-line, all the sages' heart-source — how to meet them here? The Caishi ferry's wind and waves still: fishing boats in twos and threes — one shout, one staff-crack, down from the seat, and Jiguang Huo verses the wind-and-flag case: not the wind moving, not the flag moving — is it wind, is it flag? The twos and threes crane to look, till the one watching from the side rules it, and heart and bone spit out cold.

Senses.Explanation: An ‘injustice to the buddhas of the three times’ is the adverse verdict in the paired warning that explaining scripture by following its wording wrongs the buddhas, while departing from scripture by one word joins demonic speech. The uses set a double demand rather than prohibit scripture. Yezhu compares wording-bound explanation to taking an image from a mirror or fishing for the sky in water; Shanhui says one dies miserably here; Zhanran and Tian’an answer the challenge instead of supplying another explanation. Feiyin uses the warning while discussing the printing of scripture, and Baichi deliberately refuses both halves while still prescribing recitation.
Senses.Note: The formula rejects captivity to scriptural wording, not scripture itself; it must not be expanded into a general anti-text doctrine.

Senses.Explanation: A title-of-honor string invoking all the thus-come ones of past, present, and future as one body, proclaimed in verse and hall address across the corpus. Hongzhi Zhengjue tells the assembly that with neither is nor is-not, neither joined nor parted, the thus-come ones of the three times together proclaim this very meaning; Zhongfeng Mingben opens his instruction with the teaching's word that they all appeared in the world for the one great matter; and Liao'an Qingyu works it into verse for a visiting guest — one tongue for all the three times, nothing to say in the whole canon. Gulin Qingmao's matched reply verse sings one nature for the three times with nothing left over for the stirring and wriggling; Weilin Daopei, consecrating the three-times statues, points out the one truth-body whose lit radiance shows its bearing; Konggu Daocheng tells the hall that apart from empty and not-empty they are all one alike; Yezhu Fuhui tells the layman straight that the ten kinds of beings are a dream and the three-times thus-come ones its dreamers; and Yunwai Xingze, at the frost-wood hall, has the original face with nowhere to hide and the three-times thus-come ones' mouths gone dry.

SearchAliases: the buddhas of the three times do not know it; cats and white oxen do
三世諸佛不知有，黧奴白牯卻知有
三世諸佛不知有，貍奴白牯卻知有
Senses.Note: Nanquan says that the buddhas of the three times do not know it, while cats and white oxen do. Sanyi asks what their knowing amounts to; Yingning takes it as a call to move among unlike beings. Tianran values Nanquan's refusal to fear the small. Feiyin answers with horns and a dusty face, Yi'an raises his staff into the animals' company, and Dabo uses the contrast to unsettle holy and ordinary. The animal image is a challenge to how knowing is lived. The alternate graph spelling uses the dark-cat form; both forms are the same Nanquan saying across distinct later uses.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J33/J33nB286.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Yingningjing. Yingning Jing quotes Nanquan Puyuan's contrast between the Buddhas and cats and white oxen. He says that to carry forward the teaching one must know how to move among different kinds of beings, then asks whether anyone understands Nanquan's way of acting. A layman spins away; Yingning shouts, calls the move wild jumping and strikes his staff. The exact line is Nanquan's quoted voice, while the layman's action and Yingning's response show this sermon applying it rather than explaining away the animals.

Tianran of Mount Lu raises several older sayings about recognizing the matter and then quotes Nanquan Puyuan on Buddhas not knowing while cats and white oxen know. Tianran says he admires Nanquan for not fearing what is great or belittling what is small, because Nanquan knows the cause of the illness. He asks his assembly what that cause is and returns to his own larger teaching. The exact contrast is Nanquan's cited saying; Tianran's present praise and question are a separate appraisal, and the saying leaves its object unstated.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J26/J26nB178.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Feiyin. At a hall sermon requested to honor a lay supporter's deceased parents, Feiyin Tongrong says even a broad understanding of mind and ordinary beings is only an entry point. He then voices the line that the Buddhas of three times do not know it but cats and white oxen do, and develops it through images of horns, dust-covered faces and the ending of holy-versus-ordinary distinctions. Later he restates the two halves with separate gestures of descent and ascent and asks what the old masters meant. The phrase is Feiyin's present use of an inherited contrast; neither use supplies a single fixed referent for it.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J37/J37nB394.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Yi’an. Yi'an Shanzan opens a short instruction by voicing the contrast between Buddhas who do not know it and cats and white oxen who do. He picks up his staff and tells the assembly to look: the Buddhas have gone into the company of those animals. He asks why, then says the two portions differ and are brought back under the preceding heading. The exact line is his present teaching turn; the staff gesture and follow-up complicate a fixed division between Buddhas and animals.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J40/J40nB472.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Daboqian. After a monk asks Dabo Qian about the mind of a practitioner, Dabo replies with a flowering tree, challenges the monk's elaborations and strikes when the monk hesitates. Dabo then addresses the assembly with the Buddhas-and-animals contrast and extends it: a golden-maned lion enters a pack of wild foxes, which all roar like lions. He says recognition here crosses the divide between ordinary and holy. The exact phrase is Dabo's present sermon after the exchange, not the monk's question; its object remains unnamed in the quoted formula.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J27/J27nB190.xml). Dharma Platform of Chan Master Shiyu. Shiyu Mingfang quotes Nanquan Puyuan saying that the buddhas of the three times do not know it while the dark cat and white ox do. Shiyu asks his assembly what the animals know, then asks why he does not name the present year while naming the years on either side. He suddenly extends his hand, asks how it compares with the Buddha's hand, and strikes the staff. The quoted contrast is Nanquan's; Shiyu uses the question and gestures to keep its unspecified object from becoming a ready definition.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J27/J27nB197.xml). Essentials of the Recorded Sayings of Master Wu Yi of Boshan. Wuyi Yuanlai first recounts several older Chan exchanges and then explicitly introduces Nanquan Puyuan's saying about buddhas, dark cat and white ox. He describes old Wang, Nanquan, as moving among unlike beings and adds a verse for each half: one gathers moonlight at a shadowless tree, the other cuts white clouds in a valley that does not answer. Wuyi asks who understands this. The complete pair is Nanquan's quoted voice; Wuyi's animal image and verse are his present appraisal, not another independent original saying.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J29/J29nB249.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Fangrongxi. After answering a monk's questions about host and guest, Fangrong Ruxi turns to his assembly and cites what he calls an old saying: the buddhas of the three times do not know it, while the dark cat and white ox do. He says knowing and not knowing share a source of benefit and danger, yet he accepts neither as a position. He asks whether the matter lies in retreat dates, staff and whisk, eating and drinking, or receiving and sending guests, then says that when speech is exhausted it is better to hold the tongue and settle the mind. The local quotation does not name its old speaker; parallel records attribute the pair to Nanquan, while Fangrong supplies this sermon's live challenge.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J32/J32nB272.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Hongzhi Jue of Tiantong Jingde Monastery, Mingzhou. Hongzhi Zhengjue sets Nanquan Puyuan's saying among a sequence of old cases to which he gives his own verse responses. Tianran of Mount Lu raises several older sayings about recognizing the matter and then quotes Nanquan Puyuan on Buddhas not knowing while cats and white oxen know. Tianran says he admires Nanquan for not fearing what is great or belittling what is small, because Nanquan knows the cause of the illness. He asks his assembly what that cause is and returns to his own larger teaching. The exact contrast is Nanquan's cited saying; Tianran's present praise and question are a separate appraisal, and the saying leaves its object unstated.

ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J26/J26nB178.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Feiyin. At a hall sermon requested to honor a lay supporter's deceased parents, Feiyin Tongrong says even a broad understanding of mind and ordinary beings is only an entry point. He then voices the line that the Buddhas of three times do not know it but cats and white oxen do, and develops it through images of horns, dust-covered faces and the ending of holy-versus-ordinary distinctions. Later he restates the two halves with separate gestures of descent and ascent and asks what the old masters meant. The phrase is Feiyin's present use of an inherited contrast; neither use supplies a single fixed referent for it.

Yi'an Shanzan opens a short instruction by voicing the contrast between Buddhas who do not know it and cats and white oxen who do. ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J40/J40nB472.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Daboqian. After a monk asks Dabo Qian about the mind of a practitioner, Dabo replies with a flowering tree, challenges the monk's elaborations and strikes when the monk hesitates. Dabo then addresses the assembly with the Buddhas-and-animals contrast and extends it: a golden-maned lion enters a pack of wild foxes, which all roar like lions. He says recognition here crosses the divide between ordinary and holy. The exact phrase is Dabo's present sermon after the exchange, not the monk's question; its object remains unnamed in the quoted formula.

ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J27/J27nB190.xml). Dharma Platform of Chan Master Shiyu. Shiyu Mingfang quotes Nanquan Puyuan saying that the buddhas of the three times do not know it while the dark cat and white ox do. Shiyu asks his assembly what the animals know, then asks why he does not name the present year while naming the years on either side. He suddenly extends his hand, asks how it compares with the Buddha's hand, and strikes the staff. The quoted contrast is Nanquan's; Shiyu uses the question and gestures to keep its unspecified object from becoming a ready definition.

ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J27/J27nB197.xml). Essentials of the Recorded Sayings of Master Wu Yi of Boshan. Wuyi Yuanlai first recounts several older Chan exchanges and then explicitly introduces Nanquan Puyuan's saying about buddhas, dark cat and white ox. He describes old Wang, Nanquan, as moving among unlike beings and adds a verse for each half: one gathers moonlight at a shadowless tree, the other cuts white clouds in a valley that does not answer. ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J29/J29nB249.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Fangrongxi. After answering a monk's questions about host and guest, Fangrong Ruxi turns to his assembly and cites what he calls an old saying: the buddhas of the three times do not know it, while the dark cat and white ox do. He says knowing and not knowing share a source of benefit and danger, yet he accepts neither as a position. He asks whether the matter lies in retreat dates, staff and whisk, eating and drinking, or receiving and sending guests, then says that when speech is exhausted it is better to hold the tongue and settle the mind. The local quotation does not name its old speaker; parallel records attribute the pair to Nanquan, while Fangrong supplies this sermon's live challenge.

Senses.Explanation: The buddhas of the three times do not know it, but cats and white oxen do reverses the expected hierarchy of knowing. A lamp preserves Nanquan's saying inside Dawei's explicit quotation, after which Dawei challenges both sides of the contrast. In the stronger Ancient Venerables record, Cuiyan states the same contrast in his own hall address, raises the whisk, and says the cats and white oxen are there radiating light and shaking the earth. These are distinct uses, not parallel recensions. Entries.SourceTerm: 三世諸佛被我一口吞盡

Senses.PreferredTarget: I have swallowed the Buddhas of all three times in one mouthful
SearchAliases: i have swallowed the buddhas of all three times in one mouthful
Senses.Note: Huisi answers Zhigong's call to teach by saying he has swallowed the buddhas of the three times and so sees no beings to save. The case compilation and later teachers test that reply against further questioning, solitary practice, a shouted denial, and a hypothetical encounter in the street. Huisi is the named older speaker throughout; the surrounding critiques belong to later voices.

Occurrences.Kwic: 羅龍打鳳，奈何鱗甲羽毛總在裏許，逃生無路？若是靈禽異獸，決定別有生涯。保寧勇云：玄沙道：大士只認得個昭昭靈靈。洞山道：你衲僧家白日還打睡麼？者兩轉語。誰言世上無仙客？須信壺中別有天。保寧亦有一偈：要眠時即眠，要起時即起。水洗面皮光，啜茶溼却嘴。大海紅塵飛，平地波濤起。阿呵阿呵呵，囉哩哩囉哩。崇先奇云：大小傅大士話作兩橛，在衲僧門下自救不了。何故？須知遠烟浪，別有好商量。南嶽慧思禪師因誌公令人傳語云：何不下山教化眾生？目視雲漢作麼？思曰：三世諸佛被我一口吞盡，何處更有眾生可教化？五祖戒代誌公又傳語云：更說道理看。報慈遂徵云：且道是山上語？山下語？雪竇顯云：有什麼屎臭氣？翠巖芝云：思大祇見錐頭利，不見鑿頭方。天聖泰云：思大祇知開口，寶公平地喫交。雲居舜云：思大和尚，誌公未傳語前，猶較些子。保寧勇別思大語云：傳語法師，合取狗口。雲居莊云：兩個漢總與一坑埋却，不為分外。雖然，也不得草草。良久，云：雲自帝鄉出，水從江漢流。獅林則云：一人拖泥帶水，一人斂手縮脚，徐六擔板遭人點檢。召眾云：寶公、思大二
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X66/X66n1296.xml). Compilation of the School Gate’s “Raising Old Cases”. The case compilation says that Zhigong sent a messenger to ask Nanyue Huisi why he stayed on the mountain gazing at the clouds instead of descending to teach living beings. Huisi replies that he has swallowed the buddhas of the three times in one mouthful and asks what beings remain to teach. The collection then gathers contrary responses: Wuzu Jie demands a further account, Baoci Sui questions whether this is speech from the mountain or below it, and other masters challenge Huisi's confidence. The exact boast is Huisi's quoted answer; the later comments test whether it can stand outside the original exchange.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J25/J25nB171.xml). Recorded Sayings of Monk Tianyin. In a teaching for his disciple Yinzhong, Tianyin Yuanxiu praises the student's years of steadfast practice on the mountain, but says resolve must reach beyond both buddhas and ancestors. He recalls Zhigong urging Nanyue Huisi to leave his mountain and teach; Huisi answers that he has swallowed the buddhas of all three times, leaving no beings to save. Tianyin says Huisi was not merely clinging to solitary withdrawal: the reply cuts through fixed distinctions of holy and ordinary, delusion and awakening. He tells his student to examine old cases closely until understanding and conduct both become real. Huisi speaks the exact line; Tianyin applies it to the disciple's practice.

ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J25/J25nB171.xml). Recorded Sayings of Monk Tianyin. In a teaching for his disciple Yinzhong, Tianyin Yuanxiu praises the student's years of steadfast practice on the mountain, but says resolve must reach beyond both buddhas and ancestors. He recalls Zhigong urging Nanyue Huisi to leave his mountain and teach; Huisi answers that he has swallowed the buddhas of all three times, leaving no beings to save. Tianyin says Huisi was not merely clinging to solitary withdrawal: the reply cuts through fixed distinctions of holy and ordinary, delusion and awakening. He tells his student to examine old cases closely until understanding and conduct both become real. Huisi speaks the exact line; Tianyin applies it to the disciple's practice.

The exact boast is Huisi's quoted answer; the later comments test whether it can stand outside the original exchange. In a teaching for his disciple Yinzhong, Tianyin Yuanxiu praises the student's years of steadfast practice on the mountain, but says resolve must reach beyond both buddhas and ancestors. He recalls Zhigong urging Nanyue Huisi to leave his mountain and teach; Huisi answers that he has swallowed the buddhas of all three times, leaving no beings to save. Tianyin says Huisi was not merely clinging to solitary withdrawal: the reply cuts through fixed distinctions of holy and ordinary, delusion and awakening. He tells his student to examine old cases closely until understanding and conduct both become real. Huisi speaks the exact line; Tianyin applies it to the disciple's practice. Tian'an Sheng says that someone at a solitary peak can still meet others at a busy crossroads, then raises Zhigong's challenge to Nanyue Huisi: why not descend from the mountain to teach living beings? Huisi answers that he has swallowed the buddhas of all three times and asks who remains to teach. Tian'an teases Huisi for boasting with a wide mouth and says pressure made him spill everything. Asked the same question himself, Tian'an would instead answer with the contrast between a great bird and sparrows or a frog and the sea, leaving the questioner to doubt for thirty years. The headword is Huisi's old reply; Tian'an's alternative is his present response. After an exchange in which a monk asks about moving freely beyond two constraints and Yunwai Ze strikes him, Yunwai raises the old case of Zhigong asking Nanyue Huisi why he will not descend to teach. Huisi says he has swallowed the buddhas of all three times and asks what beings remain to save. Yunwai shouts, tells the assembly that without his shout they would all be goods inside Huisi's dark belly, and says he sees neither buddhas to swallow nor beings to save. The quoted boast is Huisi's; Yunwai uses the shout and denial to keep his hearers from settling into it. Shixi Xinyue first contrasts lively activity in a busy street with quiet work in an old temple, then quotes Zhigong asking Nanyue Huisi why he will not leave the mountain to teach. Huisi answers that he has swallowed the buddhas of the three times in one mouthful, so what beings could he teach? Shixi says Huisi may think himself remarkable on a solitary peak, but imagines a thrown roof tile striking him at the crossroads and turning him bodily around. The street blow is a hypothetical test of the old mountain reply, not an event reported as having happened; the exact swallowed-buddhas line remains Huisi's quoted voice.

Senses.Note: In Xiaoyin Daxin’s entry-hall address preserved by a later anthology, he tests the Baoshou and Sansheng case, then answers what settled arrival looks like with a three-piece robe beyond green ridges and aloeswood incense amid white clouds. Xiaoyin speaks the first use, preserved in a Tier3 anthology; Guxue speaks independently in his Tier2 record. Two source contexts survive, so the reading is provisional.

Senses.PreferredTarget: When three people travel together, one must be wise.
Senses.Note: The local exchange governs each application; uncertain imagery and memorial claims are kept qualified.

Occurrences.Kwic: 三僧參，師曰：「三人同行，必有一智。誰是其人？」一僧曰：「不敢妄抵對和尚。」師曰：「不是。」問第二僧：「你是智者麼？」僧便喝。師搖手曰：「亦不是。」第三位便作禮。師曰：「你卻妥當。教侍者點碗茶來。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J39/J39nB454.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Pinjixiang. When three monks arrive, Pinjixiang Zhixiang says that among three traveling together there must be one wise person, and asks who it is. The first declines to make an unfounded reply and is rejected; the second shouts and is also rejected. The third bows, and Pinjixiang calls that fitting and asks the attendant to bring tea. The headword opens an actual examination of these visitors. In this instance a bow is accepted where a disclaimer and a shout are not, but the scene supplies no universal rule that bowing is always the wise response or that one visitor possesses wisdom independently of the exchange.

ContextActors.GrammarEvidence: 三僧參 introduces three visitors, subsequently distinguished as first speaker, second monk and third visitor; no personal names are supplied.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師遊方時，與二僧偕行，至谷隱薛大頭處，問：三人同行，必有一智。如何是一智？二僧無語。師立下肩，應聲便喝。薛舉拳作相撲勢。師云：不勞再勘。薛拽杖趂出。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X78/X78n1554.xml). Praise of the Orthodox Lineage of the Five Houses. The biography of Zhenjing Kewen recounts his arrival with two fellow travelers at Xue Datou's place at Guyin. Xue asks which is the one wise person among three. The other two cannot answer; Kewen puts down his load and shouts. Xue raises a fist as if wrestling, Kewen says there is no need to examine him again, and Xue chases him out with a staff. The quoted question belongs to the named host, Xue Datou, not to the biographical subject Kewen. Its force is shown in the reciprocal shout, posture and pursuit; the ending should not be flattened into either an explicit approval or a simple expulsion for failure.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J28/J28nB202.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Baichi. Baichi Xingyuan asks three newly arrived visitors which of them is the wise one, citing the maxim about three people traveling together. Occurrences.Kwic: 一日，新到三人來參，師云：「三人同行，必有一智，智不到處，道將一句來。」僧無語，師云：「智不在言，第二箇如何？」又無語，師云：「第三箇漆桶道看。」又無語，師云：「卻是老僧罪過，且坐喫茶。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J32/J32nB273.xml). Recorded Sayings of Monk Qianyan. Qianyan Yuanzhang addresses three newcomers with the maxim, then asks for a sentence where wisdom does not reach. The first is silent; he says wisdom is not in words and asks the second. The second and third also remain silent, the last being called a lacquer bucket. Qianyan finally takes the fault upon himself and invites them to sit for tea. The headword supplies the opening expectation which his next question immediately unsettles. Neither the statement that wisdom is not verbal nor the final hospitality turns the three silences into an explicitly certified attainment.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (T/T47/T47n1994A.xml). Recorded Sayings of Monk Fanghui of Yangqi. Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X67/X67n1303.xml). Senses.Explanation: ‘Three people attest that a turtle has become a soft-shelled turtle’ makes repeated testimony produce an absurd change of identity. Linquan Conglun’s record names Dasui Fazhen, then explains that a treasure in darkness cannot be seen without a lamp. Both named attributions are therefore shown. The second animal is the soft-shelled turtle. One record names Xianglin as the answerer; another names Dasui.

Senses.PreferredTarget: Two thirds of the time have already passed, yet the bright point of the mind remains unwiped
SearchAliases: two thirds of the time have already passed, yet the bright point of the mind remains unwiped
Senses.Note: Xuedou's verse says time is passing while the bright point remains unpolished and the person will not turn back. Qianyan asks whether polishing is even the right task; Songyuan praises Xuedou but objects to where he stops; Wuzhun answers from fire and ruin; Pingshi calls the situation a grave illness; Gulin tests his own reading against a tide. Wuzhun's passage names only an old speaker locally, although parallel records identify Xuedou.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J32/J32nB273.xml). Recorded Sayings of Monk Qianyan. Qianyan Yuanzhang recalls Xuedou Chongxian's four-line verse: much of the allotted time has passed, the bright point of the spirit terrace has not been polished, and one goes on day after day without turning back. Qianyan asks his assembly whether that point should be polished or left unpolished. No one answers, so he tells them to return to the hall for tea. Xuedou is the speaker of the quoted verse; Qianyan makes its image a live question rather than offering polishing as a settled method.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X70/X70n1377.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Songyuan Chongyue. In a hall talk, Songyuan Chongyue cites Xuedou Chongxian's verse about spent time, the unpolished bright point, and the person who will not turn back. Songyuan credits Xuedou with the power to turn heaven and earth and cut through iron, yet says the old master should not have sat down at just this point. He ends with a shout. Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X70/X70n1382.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Wuzhun Shifan. Wuzhun Shifan opens a hall talk by reciting the four-line warning that time is passing while the bright point remains unpolished and the person refuses to turn back. He says the old speaker exhausted his strength but only scratched an itch at Jingshan. Wuzhun then turns to his own ordeal: fire and ruin drove him into the world, and on returning he worked among rubble with earth and water, feeling that even his nose and eyes were lost and that he could no longer make a whole person. The local source calls the verse maker only an old person; parallel records identify Xuedou. Wuzhun's present reply uses his loss to test the verse's urgency.

Occurrences.Kwic: 須託境依人，人境既以一如，道業自然成辦。山僧九十日已前與汝諸人同一安居，九十日已後與汝諸人同一自恣，行住坐臥、語默動靜與諸人初無絲毫間隔，若是宗乘邊事，未甞蹉口道著。何故？雙峰不曾引人落草。復舉：翠岩參和尚示眾云：一夏與兄弟東語西話，看翠岩眉毛在麼？頌云：翠岩眉毛在不在？山未為高海未深。一曲無絃千古意，相逢誰是好知音？解夏，上堂。鵝護雪，臘人冰，此地無金二兩，俗人沽酒三升。拍禪牀，堪笑暮雲歸未合，遠山無數碧層層。上堂，舉：雪竇和尚偈云：三分光陰二早過，靈臺一點不揩磨，貪生逐日區區去，喚不回頭爭奈何？師云：膏肓之疾固不足以發藥，然雙峰用處也要諸人共知。便下座。中秋，上堂。吾心似秋月，碧潭清皎潔，無物堪比倫，教我如何說？師云：寒山子與麼道，大似抱贓呌屈。便下座。為雲山劉氏孺人對靈，小參。若論此事，譬如秋潭月影、靜夜鐘聲，隨扣擊以無虧、觸波瀾而不散，諸佛悟之而成佛、眾生迷之而受生。迷諸佛之所悟者，是名眾生；悟眾生之所迷者，故曰諸佛。心、佛及眾生，是三無差別。者箇道裡如人飲水，冷煖自知，說似人不得、呈似人
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X70/X70n1393.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Pingshi Rudi. Pingshi Rudi explicitly raises Xuedou Chongxian's verse in a hall talk: two parts of the time have passed, the bright point has not been polished, and a person hurrying after life will not turn back. Pingshi calls this a disease lodged deep enough that medicine may no longer help, but says his own way of using the case should still be known to the assembly; he then descends from the seat. Xuedou voices the cited warning, while Pingshi treats it as a severe diagnosis and invites scrutiny of his response rather than prescribing literal polishing.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X71/X71n1412.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Gulin Qingmao. Gulin Qingmao quotes Xuedou Chongxian's verse about dwindling time, an unpolished bright point, and the person who will not turn back. Gulin says that even this refusal to turn back makes the buddhas of the three times and the six ancestral teachers fellow practitioners. He then faults his own high-sounding reading for still following an old track and answers with a warning: someone who does not know how to ride the tide should not enter the great waves. Xuedou speaks the exact verse; Gulin's present expansion and self-correction test what it means to heed it.

ClaimAnchors.Kwic: 須託境依人，人境既以一如，道業自然成辦。山僧九十日已前與汝諸人同一安居，九十日已後與汝諸人同一自恣，行住坐臥、語默動靜與諸人初無絲毫間隔，若是宗乘邊事，未甞蹉口道著。何故？雙峰不曾引人落草。復舉：翠岩參和尚示眾云：一夏與兄弟東語西話，看翠岩眉毛在麼？頌云：翠岩眉毛在不在？山未為高海未深。一曲無絃千古意，相逢誰是好知音？解夏，上堂。鵝護雪，臘人冰，此地無金二兩，俗人沽酒三升。拍禪牀，堪笑暮雲歸未合，遠山無數碧層層。上堂，舉：雪竇和尚偈云：三分光陰二早過，靈臺一點不揩磨，貪生逐日區區去，喚不回頭爭奈何？師云：膏肓之疾固不足以發藥，然雙峰用處也要諸人共知。便下座。中秋，上堂。吾心似秋月，碧潭清皎潔，無物堪比倫，教我如何說？師云：寒山子與麼道，大似抱贓呌屈。便下座。為雲山劉氏孺人對靈，小參。若論此事，譬如秋潭月影、靜夜鐘聲，隨扣擊以無虧、觸波瀾而不散，諸佛悟之而成佛、眾生迷之而受生。迷諸佛之所悟者，是名眾生；悟眾生之所迷者，故曰諸佛。心、佛及眾生，是三無差別。者箇道裡如人飲水，冷煖自知，說似人不得、呈似人
ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X70/X70n1393.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Pingshi Rudi. Pingshi Rudi explicitly raises Xuedou Chongxian's verse in a hall talk: two parts of the time have passed, the bright point has not been polished, and a person hurrying after life will not turn back. Pingshi calls this a disease lodged deep enough that medicine may no longer help, but says his own way of using the case should still be known to the assembly; he then descends from the seat. Xuedou voices the cited warning, while Pingshi treats it as a severe diagnosis and invites scrutiny of his response rather than prescribing literal polishing.

ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X71/X71n1412.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Gulin Qingmao. Gulin Qingmao quotes Xuedou Chongxian's verse about dwindling time, an unpolished bright point, and the person who will not turn back. Gulin says that even this refusal to turn back makes the buddhas of the three times and the six ancestral teachers fellow practitioners. He then faults his own high-sounding reading for still following an old track and answers with a warning: someone who does not know how to ride the tide should not enter the great waves. Xuedou speaks the exact verse; Gulin's present expansion and self-correction test what it means to heed it.

Senses.Explanation: Xuedou warns that much of the allotted time has already passed while the bright point of the spirit terrace remains unpolished. Four sources name him; Wuzhun locally calls the verse maker only an old person. Later teachers question both the urgency and the idea that polishing offers a ready method. Qianyan Yuanzhang recalls Xuedou Chongxian's four-line verse: much of the allotted time has passed, the bright point of the spirit terrace has not been polished, and one goes on day after day without turning back. Qianyan asks his assembly whether that point should be polished or left unpolished. No one answers, so he tells them to return to the hall for tea. Xuedou is the speaker of the quoted verse; Qianyan makes its image a live question rather than offering polishing as a settled method. In a hall talk, Songyuan Chongyue cites Xuedou Chongxian's verse about spent time, the unpolished bright point, and the person who will not turn back. Songyuan credits Xuedou with the power to turn heaven and earth and cut through iron, yet says the old master should not have sat down at just this point. He ends with a shout. The exact couplet is Xuedou's quoted line; Songyuan's praise, objection, and shout challenge any fixed resting place in the warning. Wuzhun Shifan opens a hall talk by reciting the four-line warning that time is passing while the bright point remains unpolished and the person refuses to turn back. He says the old speaker exhausted his strength but only scratched an itch at Jingshan. Wuzhun then turns to his own ordeal: fire and ruin drove him into the world, and on returning he worked among rubble with earth and water, feeling that even his nose and eyes were lost and that he could no longer make a whole person. The local source calls the verse maker only an old person; parallel records identify Xuedou. Wuzhun's present reply uses his loss to test the verse's urgency. Pingshi Rudi explicitly raises Xuedou Chongxian's verse in a hall talk: two parts of the time have passed, the bright point has not been polished, and a person hurrying after life will not turn back. Pingshi calls this a disease lodged deep enough that medicine may no longer help, but says his own way of using the case should still be known to the assembly; he then descends from the seat. Xuedou voices the cited warning, while Pingshi treats it as a severe diagnosis and invites scrutiny of his response rather than prescribing literal polishing. Gulin Qingmao quotes Xuedou Chongxian's verse about dwindling time, an unpolished bright point, and the person who will not turn back. Gulin says that even this refusal to turn back makes the buddhas of the three times and the six ancestral teachers fellow practitioners. He then faults his own high-sounding reading for still following an old track and answers with a warning: someone who does not know how to ride the tide should not enter the great waves. Xuedou speaks the exact verse; Gulin's present expansion and self-correction test what it means to heed it.

Complete Five Lamps, Huanglong Huinan section: in a hall address Huanglong declares sacred and ordinary feelings exhausted and true constancy exposed. He lifts his whisk, saying it leaps to the Heaven of the Thirty-Three and pulls Shakra's nose free. His ensuing figure claps and laughs at the scarcity of people who recognize good and bad; Huanglong strikes the teaching seat and descends. The heaven is the extravagant reach of his raised whisk within this address, distinct from the preceding staff instruction.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J26/J26nB178.xml). Feiyin's Recorded Sayings, hall address: after questions about the four ways of taking person and environment, Feiyin Tongrong sets out successive claims of freedom. Even riding through countless continents and stumbling in the Heaven of the Thirty-Three, he says, establishes a nest where there was none and creates gain and loss. Raising his staff, he instead demands immediate acknowledgment here and concludes with mountains and waters returning to their source. The heaven belongs to a freedom claim that Feiyin immediately tests and overturns.

Outline Record of the Successive Patriarchs, Yu'an Zhiji's rain-prayer scripture address: Yu'an raises Muzhou's exchange about luminous clouds while reading the Flower Ornament scripture. Saying he would answer differently at Puci, Yu'an offers a fan leaping to the Heaven of the Thirty-Three, striking Shakra's nose, and an East Sea carp struck so that rain pours down. He ends with harvest songs and paired ears of grain. The inherited fan image becomes his present response at a communal prayer for rain.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X79/X79n1557.xml). Essential Compendium of the United Lamp, Xinghua Cunjiang section: Xinghua warns the assembly against blind, disorderly shouting in the corridor and latrine. Even if their shout throws him up to the Heaven of the Thirty-Three and back down lifeless, he says, on recovering he will calmly tell them they have not arrived. The heaven measures the spectacular force that still fails his test; it is not an invitation to seek a powerful shout for its own sake.

Recorded Sayings of Ancient Venerable Masters, Yunmen section: while raising the teaching of insentient things, Yunmen hears the bell and says Shakyamuni is teaching. In a later short deployment he strikes the fire stove with his staff; as the gathering watches, he says the stove leaps to the Heaven of the Thirty-Three and asks whether they see. Yushan's Recorded Sayings, Qingyun evening instruction at winter solstice: after exchanges about Huangbo's blows and the increasing cold, Yushan Shangsi warns that even swift tactical skill has not escaped the realm of shadows. He brings winter's returning yang together with Yunmen's fan leaping to the Heaven of the Thirty-Three, piercing Shakra's nose and returning to Qingyun to confess. Asked to attest it, the assembly is at a loss; Yushan warns against failing to take what is seen and scatters them with blows. He adapts the inherited ascent to his present assembly.

Continued Essentials of Ancient Venerable Masters, Cuiyan Zhen section: after raising Yunmen's answer about no unusual grass before the eyes, Cuiyan Kezhen, speaking as Shanglan, asks what lies beyond the world's ordinary appearance. He lifts his staff, sends it to the Heaven of the Thirty-Three to strike Shakra's nose, describes deities passing the complaint upward, and says it is now back in his own hand. Chushi Fanqi's Recorded Sayings, Tianning hall address: Chushi raises a monk's question to Qianfeng about the road to nirvana, then the monk's appeal to Yunmen. Yunmen's quoted answer sends a fan to the Heaven of the Thirty-Three and follows with Shakra's nose, an East Sea carp and pouring rain. Chushi appraises both Qianfeng and Yunmen with white clouds for ten thousand miles and applies the same response to a challenge about his judgment. Yunmen utters the headword in the inherited reply; Chushi is its later quoter and commentator.

Senses.Explanation: The Heaven of the Thirty-Three is the celestial realm of Shakra. These addresses make a whisk, fan, staff, stove or shouted master reach that immense height, then return the challenge to the present gathering. Huanglong, Yu’an and Cuiyan use the ascent in live gestures or imagined responses; Yunmen makes a struck stove leap. Xinghua says even a shout that throws him there proves insufficient, and Feiyin warns that claiming such freedom can create another fixed position. Chushi and Yushan deploy inherited Yunmen imagery in their own addresses. A named heaven associated with Indra.

Senses.Explanation: The thirty-two marks of the perfected body, carried by the records as the visible measure that mind is set against. Mazu Daoyi, quoted in the Mirror of the School, reads the sutra's marks as born from thought and turns them into proof that the mind-made body is the house the teaching uses; Guxue Zhenzhe counts the marks among everything that fails to appear once the heart's beings flow on; Zhuanyu Guanheng tells his correspondent that at the breakthrough one may treat the marks as a dung-chunk and the dung-chunk as the marks; and Zhongfeng Mingben traces the Seeing debate back to Ananda's claim to see the marks with his eyes. Zhanran Yuancheng reads the Devadatta chapter so that the marks are won through the bad friend on the non-path; Yongming Yanshou's own collection lists the marks as the twenty-fourth benefit of the western land; Jifei Ruyi's eulogy verse hands Ananda a sweetness that is one mark short of the thirty-two; and Juyun Chuiwan Guangzhen's endowment inscription renews the marks in gold leaf on the temple's statue.

Senses.PreferredTarget: For thirty years I sought a swordsman, through many falls of leaves and new shoots
SearchAliases: for thirty years i sought a swordsman, through many falls of leaves and new shoots
三十年來尋劍客，幾迴落葉幾抽枝
for thirty years i sought a swordsman; how many times have leaves fallen and branches grown?
thirty years seeking a sword master, through leaf fall and fresh branches again and again.
Senses.Note: Lingyun begins his peach-blossom awakening verse with thirty years of seeking through repeated seasons. Feiyin and Tian'an ask why Xuansha could affirm yet question the result. Baichi and Shipu answer with their own critical verses; Neishao distinguishes the original awakening, Guishan's confirmation, and Xuansha's later challenge. The quoted search lines are Lingyun's throughout, while the evaluations belong to later teachers. Source record (X/X69/X69n1343.xml). Baojue, the roster-linked Huitang Zuxin, raises Lingyun Zhiqin's peach-blossom verse and asks a monk whether what Lingyun saw was a peach blossom. The quoted line measures Lingyun's long search; Baojue presses the present question of seeing. Source record (X/X69/X69n1350.xml). In a separate hall talk Baoning Renyong raises Lingyun's full verse, adds Xuansha's doubt, and rejects an easy reading as an abstract principle of emptiness. Lingyun voices the quoted thirty-year line; Baoning supplies the current critique. The 幾回/幾迴 and 又抽枝/幾抽枝 forms are the same opening of Lingyun Zhiqin’s peach-blossom verse. Baojue and Baoning provide two new present analyses of its seeing; keep the published canonical head and all five older contexts.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J26/J26nB178.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Feiyin. In a hall teaching after answering a monk about spring and where to place one's feet, Feiyin Tongrong raises Lingyun Zhiqin's awakening verse. Lingyun says he sought a swordsman for thirty years through falling leaves and new shoots, then saw peach blossoms and no longer doubted. Feiyin praises the long struggle but says the sight cost Lingyun his eyes, and recalls Xuansha's objection that the experience was sound yet still incomplete. Feiyin rejects several ready explanations of the objection and ends with an image of splitting Mount Hua into two roads. The exact search lines are Lingyun's quoted voice; Feiyin keeps the question of what the blossoms settled open.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J26/J26nB187.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Tian’an Sheng. In an evening address, Tian'an Sheng recalls that Lingyun Zhiqin saw peach blossoms and composed a verse about thirty years searching for a swordsman while the leaves fell and branches sprouted. The verse says that after seeing the blossoms he no longer doubted. Tian'an immediately quotes Xuansha's judgment: the insight is certainly fitting, yet Lingyun has not fully penetrated it. He asks the assembly why Xuansha would say this if the insight were fitting, or praise it if it were not. For Tian'an, meeting that tension is how a listener might encounter Lingyun directly. The verse is Lingyun's quoted speech; Tian'an poses the present test.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J28/J28nB202.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Baichi. Baichi reads Lingyun Zhiqin's peach-blossom awakening as one case in a sequence of old encounters. He quotes Lingyun's verse beginning with thirty years seeking a swordsman through many cycles of falling leaves and new shoots, and then quotes Xuansha saying the result was fitting but still incomplete. Baichi answers with his own verse: at the sight of peach blossoms the eyes are as if blinded, and the matter arose before the word incomplete was spoken. His night-road image refuses to make either Lingyun's confidence or Xuansha's rebuke a simple final verdict. The exact search lines remain Lingyun's older verse.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J34/J34nB306.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Neishaozhong. Neishao Zhong recounts Lingyun Zhiqin at Guishan, seeing peach blossoms and giving a verse that measures thirty years of searching against leaves falling and branches budding before doubt ends. Neishao writes a response verse on the awakening, then reports Guishan testing Lingyun's realization, agreeing with it, and urging him to guard it well. Jingde Transmission of the Lamp, Ezhou Zhuyu section: Zhaozhou had first declined Yunju's suggestion that he settle at an old temple site. At Zhuyu, he again hears that an old man should settle down and asks where he could live. Zhuyu replies that such an old man still does not know his dwelling place. 三十年張弓架箭，只射得半個聖人
i drew bow and set arrow for thirty years, only to shoot half a sage.
thirty years with bow drawn and arrow ready, yet i struck only half a holy man.
Senses.Note: The bow and arrow form the case’s teaching encounter; the passage reports no physical wound. Half a sage is a contested appraisal, not an anatomical description or a simple measure of attainment. Dangui is identified from his own record without a forced personal link. Source record (J/J38/J38nB410.xml). In a small hall instruction Lianfeng Su recounts Shigong Huizang aiming an arrow at Sanping and quotes Shigong's half-sage verdict. Lianfeng then calls Sanping unfinished and Shigong fruitlessly busy, using the case to warn against premature certification. 只/祇 and 個/箇 are wording and graph variants of Shigong Huizang’s half-sage verdict. The X66 original case repeats the canonical original and is excluded; only Lianfeng Su’s distinct current critique is added.

Occurrences.Kwic: 不肯承當。山齋時自打鼓，師捧鉢作舞入堂。山便擲下鼓槌曰：是第幾和？師曰：是第二和。山曰：如何是第一和？師就桶舀一杓飯便出。仙天禪師仙天禪師洛瓶和尚參，師問：甚處來？洛瓶曰：南溪。師曰：還將南溪消息來麼？曰：消即消已，息即未息。師曰：最苦是未息。洛瓶曰：且道未息箇甚麼？師曰：一回見面，千載忘名。洛瓶拂袖便出。師曰：弄死蛇手有甚麼限？三平義忠禪師三平義忠禪師師初參石鞏，鞏常張弓架箭接機。師詣法席，鞏曰：看箭。師乃撥開胸曰：此是殺人箭，活人箭又作麼生？鞏彈弓弦三下，師乃禮拜。鞏曰：三十年張弓架箭，祇射得半箇聖人。遂抝折弓箭。後參大顛，舉前話。顛曰：既是活人箭，為甚麼向弓弦上辨？師無對。顛曰：三十年後，要人舉此話也難得。師問大顛：不用指東劃西，便請直指。顛曰：幽州江口石人蹲。師曰：猶是指東劃西。顛曰：若是鳳凰兒，不向那邊討？師作禮。顛曰：若不得後句，前話也難圓。師有偈曰：即此見聞非見聞，無餘聲色可呈君。箇中若了全無事，體用何妨分不分。睦州道明尊宿睦州道明尊宿師一日晚參，謂眾曰：汝等諸人還得箇入頭處也未？若未得箇入頭處，須覓箇入頭處；若得箇入頭處，已後不得孤負老僧。時有僧出，禮拜曰：某
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X68/X68n1319.xml). Imperially Selected Recorded Sayings. The Sanping Yizhong section recounts his first encounter with Shigong Huizang, who habitually receives students by drawing a bow and setting an arrow. When Shigong calls ‘Look out for the arrow,’ Sanping opens his chest and asks about an arrow that gives life rather than kills. Shigong sounds the bowstring three times, and Sanping bows. Shigong then says that after thirty years of drawing the bow and setting the arrow he has hit only half a sage, and breaks the bow and arrow. Shigong is the exact speaker, Sanping the respondent. Sanping later reports the encounter to Dadian, whose question about recognizing the life-giving arrow in the bowstring leaves him unable to answer. The retained original therefore preserves both recognition and a further challenge. The half is an appraisal within this teaching exchange, not evidence that Sanping was physically struck or only half alive.

Occurrences.Kwic: 政問南泉：「諸方善知識還有不說似人底法也無？」泉曰：「有。」政曰：「作麼生？」曰：「不是心，不是佛，不是物。」政曰：「恁麼則說似人了也。」曰：「某甲即恁麼，和尚作麼生？」政曰：「我又不是善知識，爭知有說不說底法？」曰：「某甲不會，請和尚說。」政曰：「我大煞與汝說了也。」師云：「南泉水上生紋，百丈日中無影。」三箇夜叉不奈何一箇窮鬼，一箇窮鬼折倒了三箇夜叉。更問如何，歸堂喫茶。石鞏張弓架箭，以接學人。三平乃披胸當之曰：「此是殺人箭，活人箭又作麼生？」鞏彈弓弦三下，平禮拜。鞏曰：「三十年張弓架箭，祇射得半箇聖人。」遂拗折弓箭。師云：「為什麼不成褫到底？合掌云：『真善知識。』」活人箭向弓弦辨，石鞏當初用得全。寧可三平只半箇，誰能更說老婆禪。仰山問中邑：「如何得見佛性？」邑曰：「譬如一室有六窗，內有一獼猴，外有獼猴從東方喚狌狌，獼猴即應，如是六窗俱喚俱應。」山禮謝，起曰：「連來蒙和尚譬喻，無不曉了。更有一事，祇如內獼猴瞌睡，外獼猴欲與相見，又且如何？」邑下禪床，執仰山手作舞，曰：「狌狌與汝相見了也。」師云：「好笑！好笑！兩箇人弄一箇獼猴，至今弄不出。」龍生龍，鳳生鳳，老鼠生底挖壁洞。燒
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J38/J38nB409.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Dangui of Danxia. In the record of Dangui of Danxia, the current master raises Shigong’s encounter with Sanping and quotes the half-sage judgment before the breaking of the bow. He asks why the acknowledgment was not carried through to completion, then joins his palms and says, ‘A true good teacher.’ His own verse says to distinguish the life-giving arrow at the bowstring, credits Shigong with using it fully from the start, and prefers leaving Sanping as only half rather than adding more solicitous explanation. The exact thirty-year remark remains Shigong’s old voice. Dangui’s present question, gesture and verse form a separate response to its apparent incompleteness; the opening question should not be flattened into a final condemnation of Shigong. The source names the record’s master as Dangui, and that source-local identity is retained without supplying an unsupported personal identification.

Occurrences.Kwic: 當之。鞏云：一張弓，兩隻箭，三十年祇射得半箇聖人。俱胝因天龍一指頭禪，一生受用不盡，故凡有所問，祇竪一指。石鞏因張弓架箭而悟，故常以張弓架箭示人雲：頂敷道：道吾舞笏同人會，石鞏張弓作者諳。三平擘胸當之，一等是弄粥飯氣，不妨應時及節。佛果引三平頌云：解擘當胸箭，如何祇半人？為從途路得，所以不全身。這般說話，大似減人光彩。萬松即不然，受箭張弓處，師資本一人。不離華下路，便見洞中春。天童道：張弓底習氣不除，受箭底相席打令。所以躭源交拳，仰山女拜，為復是全提作用？為復是時節因緣？却道三十年張弓架箭，祇射得半箇聖人。萬松道：石鞏示不全之肯，天童真以己方人。還知石鞏信彩處麼？祇將日月為香餌，應手華鱗忽上鈎。第四十三則雲門法身第四十三則雲門法身舉僧問雲門：如何是清淨法身？門云：花藥欄。僧云：便恁麼去時如何？門云：金毛師子。雪竇著語云：太無端。天童拈云：賊來須打，客來須待。雲門雪竇，二俱作家。這裏莫有便恁麼去者麼？切忌撞頭磕額。師云：萬松昔在大慶壽玄悟席下，一年入室兩度，經半年纔得告香入室。室中舉問玄沙：如何是清淨法身？沙云：膿滴滴。此是玄悟之師，高郵定和尚悟處。今日看來，這清淨法身話，玄沙
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X67/X67n1307.xml). Elder Wansong’s Commentary and Chanted Remarks on Master Tiantong Jue’s Picking Up Ancient Cases: Record of Requests for Instruction. Wansong Xingxiu discusses the half-sage phrase while commenting on earlier remarks about Shigong and Sanping. He quotes an appraisal that treats Sanping as incomplete because his understanding came by a route of acquisition, but says that such talk diminishes the person. Wansong’s own verse instead makes teacher and disciple one at the receiving of the arrow and drawing of the bow. He also gives Tiantong’s criticism that the archer’s habitual action persists and the receiver merely follows suit, together with the exact thirty-year judgment. Wansong answers that Shigong is showing an incomplete assent and that Tiantong is measuring another by himself; he closes by asking where Shigong’s winning move lies and pictures catching a splendid fish with sun and moon as bait. Thus Shigong is the quoted speaker of the exact phrase, while Wansong supplies the present counter-reading. The disagreement makes the word ‘half’ something to examine, not a settled grade to copy.

Occurrences.Kwic: 又，石鞏禪師見馬祖得悟之後，只張弓架箭接人。一日，三平來參，鞏云：『看箭。』平展開胸，云：『這個是殺人箭，如何是活人箭？』鞏扣弓弦三下，平禮拜，鞏折箭，云：『三十年張弓架箭，只射得半個聖人。』平後再參大顛，舉前話，顛云：『既是活人箭，因甚向弓弦上覓？』平無語，遂折伏。後得悟，承嗣大顛。」師云：「出齏缸，入醋甕，三平未是真龍；拋弓折箭，石鞏可謂勞而無功矣。雖然，比今之學者未參學先圖印證，堂頭老漢也不審其有頭腦、無頭腦，只管將冬瓜印子印將去，以致養子不及父，家門一世衰。

Senses.PreferredTarget: thirty years later
AlternateTargets: thirty years from now
Senses.Note: A literal future interval used to put a later retelling, answer, or forecast at a distant point in time. The phrase does not by itself prescribe a thirty-year practice or waiting period.

Occurrences.Kwic: 且道。把住好放行好。三十年後逢人不得錯舉。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (T/T47/T47n1997.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Yuanwu Foguo. Yuanwu Keqin asks whether holding fast or letting go is better and tells the assembly not to cite it incorrectly when meeting someone thirty years later.

Occurrences.Kwic: 畢竟在什麼處。三十年後。待山僧換骨出來。却向爾道。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (T/T48/T48n2003.xml). Blue Cliff Record by Chan Master Yuanwu Foguo. In his commentary, Yuanwu Keqin asks where the matter ultimately lies and says that thirty years later, after this mountain monk comes out with changed bones, he will tell the listener.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師云：去聖時遙，人多懈怠，三十年後討箇師僧也難得。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X79/X79n1557.xml). Essential Compendium of the United Lamp. After Danxia circles the Chan seat and leaves, Nanyang Huizhong says that the sages are remote and people are lax, so thirty years later even finding a monk will be difficult. This is the sole retained lamp recension.

ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (T/T47/T47n1998A.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Dahui Pujue. Dahui Zonggao answers the unnamed monk's thirty-years-later forecast by saying that many people are laughing at him right now.

Senses.Explanation: Thirty years later keeps its ordinary future-time sense while serving several kinds of distant reckoning. Yuanwu Keqin warns that his question about holding fast or letting go must not be cited incorrectly when the listener meets someone thirty years later. In the Blue Cliff Record, Yuanwu postpones his answer until this mountain monk comes out with changed bones thirty years later. The lamp account of Nanyang Huizhong uses the same interval for a forecast: with the sages remote and people lax, even finding a monk will then be difficult. An unnamed monk tells Dahui Zonggao that many people will laugh thirty years later; Dahui answers that many are laughing at him right now. These uses defer a retelling, an answer, or a consequence, while Dahui's reply rejects the proposed delay; none defines a required thirty-year discipline.

Entries.SourceTerm: 三十年後，要人舉此話也難得

Senses.PreferredTarget: Thirty years from now, it will be hard to find anyone who can bring up this exchange.
AlternateTargets: After thirty years, it will be difficult to find someone able to raise this case.
SearchAliases: thirty years from now, it will be hard to find anyone who can bring up this exchange.
after thirty years, it will be difficult to find someone able to raise this case.
Senses.Note: Dadian delivers the line after Sanping cannot answer his challenge about a life-giving arrow and its bowstring. Eryin later retells that exchange and supplies a new answer to the challenge before Dadian’s verdict. The old line is Dadian’s in both sources; Eryin is the later commentator. The complete verdict has a different job from the public generic time phrase 三十年後. One current Tier2 interpretation and one older case survive, so this reading is provisional.

Occurrences.Kwic: 「撫州石鞏禪師，凡見，師以弓架箭示之。一日，三平至，鞏云：『看箭！』三平乃撥開胸云：『此是殺人箭，活人箭又作麼生？』鞏乃扣弓弦三下，平便作禮。鞏云：『三十年架一張弓、兩隻箭，只射得半個聖人。』遂拗折弓箭。平後舉似大顛，顛云：『既是活人箭，為甚麼向弓弦上辨？』平無對，顛云：『三十年後，要人舉此話也難得。』」師代云：「待伊道：『既是活人箭，為甚麼向弓弦上辨？』但云：『既從地倒，還從地起。』」

Entries.SourceTerm: 三十年行脚，今日錯為人下註脚

Senses.PreferredTarget: After thirty years of travelling, today I mistakenly supplied someone with a gloss.
SearchAliases: thirty years travelling mistakenly add a gloss
三十年行脚，今日錯為人下注脚
Senses.Note: The reported mistake is itself questioned by later masters. The phrase should not settle the encounter in advance by declaring either participant defeated. The original speaker and later appraisers remain separate. Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X81/X81n1571.xml). Complete Five Lamps (Vols. 1–33). While Zhaozhou is washing his feet at Linji’s monastery, Linji asks about the patriarch’s coming from the west. Zhaozhou points to the present washing; when Linji leans forward as though listening, Zhaozhou challenges that gesture. Linji returns to his room, and Zhaozhou makes the exact remark about thirty years of travel and mistakenly supplying a gloss. Zhaozhou is the speaker, Linji the questioner. The closing self-assessment leaves their brief contest open to the later appraisals.

The anthology preserves the old exchange and then Fayun Xiu’s current objection to a common explanation: that Zhaozhou failed to recognize Linji’s maneuver and should have struck him instead of adding a gloss. ClaimAnchors.ClaimText: 三十年行脚，今日錯為人下注脚

Senses.Explanation: After thirty years of travelling, today I mistakenly supplied someone with a gloss. While Zhaozhou is washing his feet at Linji’s monastery, Linji asks about the patriarch’s coming from the west. Zhaozhou points to the present washing; when Linji leans forward as though listening, Zhaozhou challenges that gesture. Linji returns to his room, and Zhaozhou makes the exact remark about thirty years of travel and mistakenly supplying a gloss. Zhaozhou is the speaker, Linji the questioner. The closing self-assessment leaves their brief contest open to the later appraisals. The anthology preserves the old exchange and then Fayun Xiu’s current objection to a common explanation: that Zhaozhou failed to recognize Linji’s maneuver and should have struck him instead of adding a gloss. Xiu rejects that reading, calls both men old thieves and asks which is the skillful one. The exact closing remark remains Zhaozhou’s quoted speech. Xiu’s intervention prevents its word ‘mistakenly’ from being treated as a straightforward admission that Linji simply defeated him. Another anthology records Songyuan Chongyue asking precisely where Zhaozhou supplied the wrong gloss and demanding an answer. It also attributes a verse to Gushan Gui saying that neither the foot-washing nor the listening was an arranged performance and asking when the two masters ever supplied a gloss at all. These are distinct later challenges to the old closing remark, which still belongs to Zhaozhou. They share one retained source window rather than being duplicated as separate occurrences. Zhaozhou is washing his feet when Linji asks about the patriarch coming from the west; Zhaozhou answers from that action, and Linji leans in as if listening. The selected line is Zhaozhou's own ironic claim that he has wrongly given someone an explanation. Fayun Xiu then rejects the ordinary claim that Linji tricked him and asks which old master was truly adept; his appraisal makes this copied case a current teaching test. Xiatang Huiyuan raises the old scene of Zhaozhou washing his feet while Linji asks for the patriarch's meaning. After Zhaozhou says he mistakenly supplied an explanation, Xiatang asks exactly where that supposed error lies, pauses, then gives his own answer. Zhaozhou is the selected quoted speaker; Xiatang's live question turns the line into an investigation. Songyuan Chongyue tells the same Zhaozhou–Linji foot-washing encounter and quotes Zhaozhou's mistaken-explanation line. He answers with half rain, half sun and flowering trees, then asks the listeners to locate the mistaken gloss for themselves. This is a separate present critique of Zhaozhou's quoted words, not Songyuan speaking the original line.

Senses.Explanation: Thirty blows is a fixed counted beating placed in the language of verdict and encounter. Foyan invokes Deshans old boat-rail rebuke and then assigns the count to his own listeners; Nanjian directs it at the World-Honored One; Jian Shan lets a monk off with it. Baichi and Guxue use it in current replies, while Miyun, Feiyin, and Liaozong assign it in independent appraisals of raised cases. Retained public meaning is supported by independent present uses in recorded discourse.

Xueguan Zhiyin questions a returning practitioner who claims not to have seen anyone on his travels. AlternateTargets: Thirty blows opened clear sight, with no patriarchal mind to pass on

Senses.Note: Wuming Huijing composed the couplet in a verse on Linji after meeting Ruifeng. Yuzhe later uses it to press his hall audience about direct experience, while Weilin explicitly quotes and praises the Shouchang master verse before retelling Linji at Huangbo. Yongjue authored the container that preserves Wuming biography, not this verse.

Occurrences.Kwic: 見法可名佛法，何所成就？世尊曰：汝豈不得無著性耶？文殊答曰：我即無著，豈無著性復得無著？師云：世尊三問問，問在文殊足下藏身；文殊三答答，答在毗盧頂上獨步。須知毗盧頂上不離文殊足下，文殊足下只在毗盧頂上。忽有箇人類精奇底，向這裏直下見得徹、信得及、擔荷得去，從文殊一門深入，驀直歸家，更有何事？雖然如是，只如最初入門一句作麼生？良久，云：誰為文殊？誰是文殊？示眾，師云：昔臨濟老人於黃檗手中喫棒，向大愚脇下還拳，如空合空，了無縫罅。後來壽昌師翁頌云：醍醐上味出乎乳，滴水攙中總不成，三十棒頭開正眼，何曾傳得祖師心？可謂徹骨徹髓矣。雖然如是，更須知臨濟中夏上黃檗一段因緣，今日不免舉似大眾去也。臨濟中夏上黃檗山，見檗看經，乃云：將謂是箇人，原來是箇唵黑豆老和尚。住數日，告辭，檗曰：子破夏來，何不終夏去？濟曰：某甲暫來禮拜和尚。檗便打，趂令去。濟行數里疑此事，却回終夏。後又辭檗，檗曰：甚麼處去？濟曰：不是河南，便歸河北。檗便打，濟約住與一掌，檗大笑。檗喚侍者：將百丈先師禪板几案來。濟云：侍者將火來。檗云：不然，子但將去，已後坐斷天下人舌頭去在。大眾！舉已舉了、判已判了，只如臨濟當時行數里疑

Occurrences.Kwic: 上堂。問：「眉間挂劍，截斷葛藤，是甚麼人境界？」師云：「三千劍客，恥見莊周。」乃云：「今日六月六，人間曝衣𤾣。艸堂無所蓄。」驀豎拳，云：「惟有者箇物，不屬陰陽晴雨，不受梅天擺布。見者定超三有，聞者橫機獨露。是古佛生涯，是死生窠窟，乃曹源之一滴，係鷲嶺之玉柱。用之成佛成仙，體之無聲無臭。豎窮三際，超非非想之聖輪；橫亙十方，拓無無明之坦路。」召大眾，云：「還識此物麼？海神知貴不知價，留與人間光照夜。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J27/J27nB194.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Xuezui of Zhaojue. Zhangxue Tongzui answers a monk who asks what sort of person hangs a sword between the brows and cuts through tangled creepers. His reply puts three thousand swordsmen to shame before Zhuang Zhou, answering the martial challenge with an image of overwhelming mastery. He then turns to the present day of airing clothes, says his monastery has nothing stored, and raises a fist as the one thing beyond weather and the usual oppositions. He asks the assembly to recognize it. The swordsmen line is an answer about capacity that leads into this present gesture, not a literal claim that a historical duel is occurring in the hall. The headword is rendered: Three thousand swordsmen are ashamed to face Zhuang Zhou.

Occurrences.Kwic: 舉：「三聖問雪峰：『透網金鱗以何為食？』峰云：『待汝出網來向汝道。』聖云：『一千五百人善知識，話頭也不識。』峰云：『老僧住持事繁。』」師云：「入林不動艸，入水不動波，天下宗師，一期方便。三聖雖然迴避金鉤，殊不知已吞紅線，說甚話頭不識？何故？三千劍客，恥見莊周。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J37/J37nB371.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Foyuan. Foyuan Chegang comments on Sansheng asking Xuefeng what the golden fish that has passed through the net eats. Xuefeng tells him to leave the net before he will answer; Sansheng accuses this teacher of fifteen hundred people of not understanding the question, and Xuefeng says he is busy with the monastery. Foyuan says Sansheng avoided the golden hook but has already swallowed the red line, then asks why and gives the swordsmen pair. The image caps his judgment that Sansheng's apparent evasion has not outwitted Xuefeng. It is Foyuan's later appraisal, outside both earlier speakers' words. The headword is rendered: Three thousand swordsmen are ashamed to face Zhuang Zhou.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (T/T51/T51n2077.xml). Continued Transmission of the Lamp, Anji Daochang Yougui section: Yougui raises his staff and asks whether it is seen. Elaborate discrimination and worldly ingenuity become a hair in empty space and a drop in a vast ravine; even Deshan burning his commentaries is likened to drawing a bow after the thief has gone. The couplet is his own closing answer to that demand within the staff address.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J28/J28nB219.xml). Recorded Sayings of Monk Zhuanyuheng of Purple Bamboo Grove. In an instruction to the lecturer Hanming Lei, Zhuanyu Guanheng says that large things require long preparation. He offers the three-thousand-great-thousand world-system as his measure: even its forming, abiding, breaking and emptiness each take twenty smaller eons. He compares that immense process with the work of realizing awakening and warns the student against expecting an instant, effortless mastery. The headword names the conventional great world-system in Zhuanyu's scale analogy.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J26/J26nB178.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Feiyin. After answering a layman's question about whether the Buddha's old flower gesture and Feiyin Tongrong's present hall address are the same or different, Feiyin raises his whisk. He pictures its tongue extending over the three-thousand-great-thousand world-system and bringing a teaching to all who see or hear it, then shouts and closes the address. The headword names the full spatial reach of Feiyin's imagined whisk action; the old Buddha gesture belongs to the preceding comparison.

Entries.SourceTerm: 三千年黃河清，五百載聖人出

Senses.PreferredTarget: The Yellow River clears once in three thousand years; a sage appears once in five hundred.
AlternateTargets: After three thousand years the Yellow River runs clear, and after five hundred a sage comes forth.
SearchAliases: rare clear Yellow River, rare sage appears

Occurrences.Kwic: 。「戶貼家平堪縱奪，祖翁田地深撈抹，徐引清風壯四維，拋沙撒土填溝壑。填溝壑，攧撐蹴殺黃幡綽。」上堂。舉：「牛過窗櫺，頭角四蹄俱過了，惟尾巴過不得。朱樓百尺巧妝榮，跨犢翁翁繞畫屏。一孔一毛一世界，何須尾巴度窗櫺？」資州豎幢西堂，請上堂。「菴外磨磚，真機早泄。高安築拳，汝師黃檗。隔江招手較些些，橫趨而去猶未瞥。若是烜赫兒孫，爭敢違條起例？」卓拄杖：「既逢家裏人，畢說家中話。一刀還一痕，一斧仍一劄。一掌復一拳，一腳就一踏。莫嫌老大力無筋，抹過金圈拋棘辣。諸昆仲！綱要提持，全身擔荷。三千年黃河清，五百載聖人出。」復卓拄杖，下座。上堂。「佛未出世，還有經可看麼？還有禪可參麼？還有道可學麼？既總沒有，諸人作麼生履踐？急要相投有意陳，知音何必更勞神？山河大地俱推倒，佛祖從何插腳行？」上堂。「臨濟白拈賊，萬里一條銕，東壁敲西籬，三界難拘測。與麼孤硬太煞，設有旁不肯者麼？拄杖子悄身而出，便道：『此老假佛衣，竊佛食，有來由，沒巴鼻，舌頭帝都釘，脣齒斑豹碧，曾受蒿枝拂，不涉廉纖句，一塵一佛國，一機中一的。』大眾！秖如五天通漢地，梵語雜唐言一句作麼生道？」擊拂子，「箭簇那容機返勢，懸河豈惜辯相饒
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J37/J37nB371.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Foyuan. Occurrences.Kwic: ，我無伎倆；二千年後，我有伎倆，你無伎倆。何故？入水見長人。據室橫按拄杖，顧視左右，云：有麼？有麼？卓一下，云：無人過價，打與三百。拈院疏，云：箇是大丞相親受靈山記莂底句子，付在山僧，未聞者聞、未見者見。指法座，云：坐斷報化佛頭，不落玄玅階級。竇八布衫，雲門念七。陞座，拈香祝聖，問答罷，乃云：夫為宗師者，提持綱要，接物利生，豈是細事？況茲山千載名藍，五天化境，大丞相號令明肅，出於至公。山僧既已回避無門，諸人各要知時識節。拈拄杖，云：即心即佛，非心非佛。不是心，不是佛，不是物。三千年黃河清，五百載聖人出。復舉：僧問投子：諸佛出世為一大事因緣，和尚出世當為何事？投子云：尹司空為老僧開堂。師云：投子老人可謂應機施設，不犯鋒𨦵，中峰不免因齋慶讚。一髮由來引萬鈞，全肩荷負見當人。通身手眼重拈掇，枯木華開大地春。當晚，小參。凡夫色礙，二乘空礙，菩薩色空無礙。拈拄杖，云：拄杖子列列挈挈，不入眾數，有時十字街頭橫挑布袋，有時白雲景裏打雨敲風，法隨法行，法幢隨處建立，有佛處不得住，無佛處急走過，三千里外一句全提。畢竟如何話會？卓拄杖，云：一六三四二，直言曲七一，桃李火中開，黃昏候日出。復舉
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X69/X69n1367.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Xiaoyin Daxin. At his Tianzhu temple installation under a grand minister's patronage, Xiaoyin Daxin raises his staff after an opening question and voices the same clear-river and rare-sage saying. He then recalls Touzi answer to why a master comes forth and uses it to praise this present appointment. The selected line is Daxin's own sermon, not a line uttered by Touzi.

Occurrences.Kwic: 茶去？州喚院主，主應諾。州曰：喫茶去。保福展云：趙州慣得其便。鏡清怤舉問僧云：汝作麼生會？僧便去。清云：邯鄲學唐步。雪竇顯云：這僧不是邯鄲人，為甚學唐步？若辨得出，與汝茶喫。青龍斯云：趙州老漢通身為人，不免被院主看破。趙州因僧辭，州問：甚處去？曰：諸方學佛法去。州豎拂曰：有佛處不得住，無佛處急走過。三千里外，逢人不得錯舉。曰：與麼則不去也。州曰：摘楊花，摘楊花。徑山杲云：有佛處不得住，生鐵秤錘被蟲蛀；無佛處急走過，撞著嵩山破竈墮。三千里外，逢人不得錯舉。兩個石人相耳語，恁麼則不去也。此語已徧天下。摘楊花！摘楊花！唵！摩尼達哩！吽！㗶吒！天童覺云：沉空滯跡，犯手傷鋒，俱未是衲僧去就。直須不入人行市，不上他牀榻

Occurrences.Kwic: 所以道。無邊剎海。自他不隔於毫端。十世古今。始終不移於當念。不隔處總十方為真境。不移處貫十世於目前。淨躶躶脫塵情。赤灑灑無蓋覆。直得千聖同躔萬機頓赴。還會麼。竿頭絲線從君弄。不犯清波意自殊。下座。上堂。僧問。如何是教外別傳一句。師云。問取燈籠。進云。謝師答話。師云。自領出去。進云。却是禪外別傳也。師云。三千里外過崖州。問學人不恁麼時如何。師云。莫亂統。進云。趙州庭前柏。崇寧庭前楠。是同是別。師云。莫眼華。進云。一種沒絃琴。惟師彈得妙。師云。山僧亦不承當。乃云。在天成象在地成形。日月為照臨。四時作寒暑。居谷盈谷處坑滿坑。有情則動轉施為。無情則森羅顯煥。如今在山僧拄杖頭上。指山山崩。指海海竭。點鐵成金。點金成鐵。

Occurrences.Kwic: 方能把住放行，有自由分。保寧勇頌云：堂堂好箇丈夫兒，剛被胡麻取次欺。若解奮拳張意氣，世間何處可容伊？天童覺云：青山不異，白玉無瑕。茫茫流水，擾擾黃花。有佛處纖塵不立，無佛處萬別千差。長安路上未歸客，尋溪猶自摘楊花。佛慧泉云：截斷三關過者稀，臨鋒誰解振全威？楊花摘處何人見？風送漫天似雪飛。普融平云：三千里外兩重關，衲子紛紛過者難。回首石橋南北路，楊花風散雪漫漫。龍潭信禪師在天皇三年，忽一日問云：某甲自到來，不蒙和尚指示心要。皇云：自汝到來，吾未甞不指示汝心要。師云：甚處是指示某甲心要處？皇云：汝擎茶來，吾為汝接。汝行食來，吾為汝受。汝和南時，吾便低首。何處不指示汝心要？師竚思，皇云：見即直下便見，擬思即差。

Occurrences.Kwic: 前來。待他近前，却向道去。何故？白雲乍可離青嶂，明月難教下碧空。開爐上堂，舉雪峯和尚道：世界闊一丈，古鏡闊一丈。玄沙云：火爐闊多少？雪峯云：如古鏡闊。師拈云：雪峯、玄沙父子激揚，大似泥裏洗土，若望臨際門下，遠之遠矣。且道臨濟門下如何？良久，云：看火色。上堂。拈拄杖卓一下，云：子承父業，依而行之，影響之流，三千里外。還有獨脫底麼？退後，退後，久雨不晴，妨我晒眼皮革。上堂，舉光侍者向玄沙道：師叔若參得禪，某甲打鐵舡泛海去。後玄沙住院，令人傳語光侍者：還曾打就鐵舡也未？師拈云：猛虎不食伏肉，可惜玄沙撞在光侍者網裏。冬節，上堂。節令不相饒，陽生第一爻，諸佛道長，眾生道消。拈拄杖，云：拄杖子，獨孤標，且道隨節令？不隨節令

Occurrences.Kwic: 云：三日前，五日後，若不揮劒，漁父棲巢。與麼說話，大似擔水河頭賣，光非照境，境亦非存，光境俱亡，復是何物？大慧和尚云：千年常住一朝僧。卓主丈云：竹影掃階塵不動，月穿潭底水無痕。上堂。一切法即是佛法，燈籠自灯籠，露柱自露柱；一切法不是佛法，蝦蟇吞却大象，蚯蚓咬殺麒麟，辨龍蛇，擒虎兕。穿却天下衲僧鼻孔即不問，三千里外逢人不得。錯舉一句作麼生道？以主丈畫一畫，云：星河秋一鴈，砧杵夜千家。上堂：金風扇野，玉露垂珠。葉墮林間，蛩吟砌畔。解脫門宏開八字，真實義綿亘十方。諸人眼見耳聞，一一超今邁古。向上一路，別有誵訛。槌折你腰，第一莫將來。將來不相似，禿却你舌。壁立萬仞沒商量，打刀須是邠州鐵。謝道舊，上堂。敲空作響，罕遇知

Senses.Explanation: A fixed distance that places a sentence, a sound, or a person beyond the reach of everyone present. Zhaozhou Congshen sends the departing monk past the places of buddhas and no-buddhas and bars him, that far out, from misreporting the instruction, Yuanwu Keqin pitches the borrowed claim of a transmission outside the gate past Yazhou at that remove, Zhihai Purong Daoping sings two gates standing that far out where few patch-robed ones pass, Shitian Faxun files the imitators who merely inherit the father's trade at that remove, and Zhongfeng Mingben sets one sentence at the staff tip, one at the sandal sole, and one three thousand li away. Gulin Qingmao pierces the nose-strings of the realm's patch-robed ones and bars the misreport that far out, Juelang Daosheng tells the marked monk the blow is not his affair and orders him back three thousand li, Yikui Yuankui lets only the old barbarian know without grasping and bars the misreport that far out, Xiaotang Yunfen spreads one hair-tip's pattern for those with eyes while its sound differs that far out for those with ears, and Tian'an Sheng asks how the blind of Wu, that far from the capital, could ever see the emperor's dress.

Entries.SourceTerm: 三千里外，逢人不得錯舉

Senses.PreferredTarget: Three thousand miles away, do not misstate it when you meet someone
AlternateTargets: Far from here, take care not to repeat the matter wrongly to anyone you meet
SearchAliases: three thousand miles away do not misquote
far away meet someone do not state it wrongly
Senses.Note: Luyan uses the pair to answer a monk's question about the third essential; Hanyue recasts Zhaozhou's three travel clauses; Yikui closes a retreat with it; Miaoyun shouts and places it after old case comments; Zhufeng makes it a question at a coffin rite. The distance is an image of carrying an answer into a later meeting, and each present teacher voices the line in a different practical setting.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J39/J39nB452.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Lüyan He. A monk asks Luyan He for the three mysteries and the three essentials. Luyan gives separate, surprising answers to each question; for the first two essentials he says not to stay where there is a buddha and to pass quickly where there is none. Asked for the third, he says that three thousand miles away one must not misstate it when meeting someone. He then turns to an autumn hall address on the forms before the assembly. The exact travel warning is Luyan's answer in this present exchange, using an inherited Zhaozhou line to test whether the monk can carry an answer beyond the room.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J34/J34nB299.xml). Recorded Sayings of Monk Sanfeng Zang. In a hall sermon, Hanyue Fazang revoices the three-part travel counsel associated with old Zhaozhou: do not stay where there is a buddha, pass quickly where there is none, and three thousand miles away do not misstate it when meeting someone. He inserts his own odd images after the first two clauses, then says that a word is a word and a sentence a sentence. He challenges the conclusion that this means simply not going, and ends by teasing old Zhaozhou. The full warning is voiced by Hanyue in the present sermon; Zhaozhou is the inherited source he is testing.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J37/J37nB388.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Yikui of Shending. At the closing of a retreat, Yikui Yuankui says that whether the period is long or short, its measure is awakening. He adds images of a great elephant avoiding a rabbit path and the sea refusing a dead body, then says one may allow the old teacher to understand but not merely to know. He ends with the warning that, three thousand miles away, one must not misstate it when meeting someone. Yikui speaks the exact line to the assembly at the retreat close, making the future meeting of another person a test of what the retreat has meant.

ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J34/J34nB299.xml). Recorded Sayings of Monk Sanfeng Zang. In a hall sermon, Hanyue Fazang revoices the three-part travel counsel associated with old Zhaozhou: do not stay where there is a buddha, pass quickly where there is none, and three thousand miles away do not misstate it when meeting someone. He inserts his own odd images after the first two clauses, then says that a word is a word and a sentence a sentence. He challenges the conclusion that this means simply not going, and ends by teasing old Zhaozhou. The numbered form does not by itself identify one fixed Chan teaching: Baizhang Huaihai, Wuzhu, Fenyang Shanzhao, Yunmen Wenyan, and Linji Yixuan are associated with different triads, separated below because their members and referents differ.

AlternateTargets: Baizhang's three statements

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X72/X72n1437.xml). Expanded Record of Chan Master Yongjue Yuanxian (永覺元賢禪師廣錄): Baizhang Huaihai utters the exact headword-bearing wording in the complete source unit.

Senses.Explanation: Baizhang Huaihai's three phrases form a particular three-part statement about attachment. His record distinguishes not taking hold of objects, not dwelling in non-attachment, and not constructing an understanding of that non-dwelling and non-attachment; passing through the three phrases is then named as a further test. Yongjue Yuanxian later reproduces the same three members as Baizhang's formulation. This is a different referent from the triads associated with Wuzhu, Fenyang, Yunmen, or Linji.

Senses.Explanation: Wuzhu's three-phrase teaching names a fixed set: no recollection, no thought, and no delusion. In the public exchange, the official Du Hongjian asks Wuzhu whether this is the teaching he gives. Wuzhu confirms it, maps the members to precepts, concentration, and wisdom, and refuses to make the set either simply one or simply three. The entry reports that recorded configuration without importing an outside account of what its members mean.

Senses.Explanation: Fenyang Shanzhao's three phrases are separately named for a student's exerting strength, turning the body, and intimacy. Fenyang answers a question on each member and then says that understanding these three phrases distinguishes the three mysteries while three essentials still remain. Yongjue Yuanxian later calls Fenyang's set a mass of fire that cannot be approached yet is not other than fire when turned away from. These statements identify a named Fenyang configuration rather than a generic three-part form.

Senses.Explanation: The set transmitted as Yunmen's Three Phrases consists of enclosing heaven and earth, cutting off the myriad streams, and following the waves and pursuing the swells. Jiuding Jixing Huiquan names all three as Yunmen's set. Sanfeng Hancang repeats the same members while challenging the later formulation and attributes the three-part wording to Deshan Yuanming. The historical qualification matters: the corpus conventionally names the triad for Yunmen while also recording Deshan Yuanming as the person who separated Yunmen's words into these three phrases.

Senses.Explanation: Linji Yixuan's three phrases are a ranked set of first, second, and third phrases. Linji says that attainment in the first permits teaching buddhas and patriarchs, attainment in the second permits teaching humans and gods, and attainment in the third does not suffice to save oneself. Yunmen Wenyan later raises Linji's three-phrase saying and asks a stupa keeper which phrase had been attained by the person inside the stupa. The ranking and its cross-house use distinguish this referent from every other triad in the entry.

Occurrences.Kwic: 衲僧，豈不快哉！門云：你身如椰子大，開得如許大口。師便禮拜。住後，上堂曰：言無展事，語不投機；承言者喪，滯句者迷。還會得麼？你衲僧分上到這裏，須具擇法眼始得。只如洞山恁麼道，也有一場過，且道過在甚麼處？林泉道：再犯不容。僧問：如何是佛？師答：麻三斤。還有這裏辨錙銖、知輕重的麼？佛身既充法界，法性何處不周？剎剎如然，塵塵皆爾，拶破面門，磕傷額角，不免教人點檢道：當局者迷，傍觀者哂。況杭州興教小壽禪師亦云：山河及大地，全露法王身。林泉雖恁離堅合異，莫便尋言逐句，識情卜度。不見道：三句外會取，六句外省去。只如到此，端的合作麼生會？良久，云：還相委悉麼？定盤星上無斤兩，莫逐高低漫度量。頌曰：三年一閏大家知，也有顢頇不記時。昨夜鴈迴沙塞冷，嚴風吹綻月中枝。師云：三百六旬，似蟻循環而不住；七十二候，如珠走盤而非停。日月如梭，春秋若箭，所以閏餘成歲，全因律呂調陽。萬松先師住仰山時，閏四月旦日，上堂云：所謂道人者，不知月之大小，不知歲之餘閏。野僧即不然，今年三百八十四日，前月大盡，此月小盡，即今閏四月一日辰末巳初，忽有箇出來道：通疏伶利，知時按節，要且無道人氣息。野僧以手掩鼻道：近後

Occurrences.Kwic: 夏。汝等諸人還知去處麼？良久，云：九旬陽焰裏，五分法身圓。端師子看楞嚴經二頌。七處徵心心不遂，懵懂阿難不瞥地。直饒徵得見無心，也是泥中洗土塊。八還之教垂來久，自古宗師各分剖。直饒還得不還時，也是蝦跳不出斗。藥山和尚問雲巖：甚處來？云：百丈來。曰：百丈有何言句？云：有時示眾云：我有一句子，百味具足。山曰：鹹即鹹味，淡即淡味，不鹹不淡是常味。作麼生是百味具足底句？巖無對。山笑曰：爭柰目前生死何？巖云：目前無生死。曰：二十年在百丈處，俗氣也不除。次日又問：海兄更說甚法？云：有時道：三句外會取，六句外省去。山曰：且喜沒交涉。又問：更說甚麼法？云：有時陞堂眾集，以拄杖打下，復召大眾，眾回首却云：是甚麼？山曰：何不早道？巖於此有省。妙喜曰：省去即不無，爭柰未出葛藤窠。琅邪覺和尚示眾云：汝等諸人在我遮裏過夏，與你點出五般病：一不得向萬里無寸草處去，二不得孤峯獨宿，三不得張弓架箭，四不得物外安身，五不得滯於生殺。何故？一處有滯，自救難為；五處若通，方名導師。汝等諸人若到諸方，遇明眼作者，與我通箇消息，貴得祖風不墜。若是常徒，即須寢息。何故？躶形國裏誇服飾，想君大殺不知時。又頌栢樹子話
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X67/X67n1309.xml). Treasury of the True Dharma Eye. He introduces the three-and-six-sentence maxim with 'have you not heard it said,' asks how it should be understood here, pauses, and gives his own weighing-scale image. The maxim's exact earlier speaker is unnamed locally; Linquan is the present user. Yunyan tells Yaoshan that Baizhang sometimes said to understand beyond three sentences and realize beyond six. Yaoshan says that has no bearing, then probes another Baizhang teaching that brings Yunyan an opening. Dahui's following appraisal says the opening still has not escaped entangling talk. Baizhang is the exact quoted speaker of the maxim; Dahui is the later critic.

Senses.Explanation: The three-inch tongue is the speaking organ in cutting and silencing formulas, while ordinary “three inches” remains a separate measure. It is often shortened in Chan exchanges to just 'the three inches.' Baoning Renyong supplies the full form: 'I have one mouth, containing a three-inch tongue; the teeth are all complete, and there is no right and wrong it does not speak' (我有一張口，內含三寸舌。牙齒總完全，是非無不說). An unnamed questioner asks Cuiyan Lingcan to speak 'without borrowing the three inches' (不借三寸。請師道。), and another unnamed questioner calls Dahui Zonggao's 'three inches' tightly guarded (老和尚三寸甚密). The omitted noun is recoverable from the explicit full form and from the predicates of speaking. The Zen bend is this use of an ordinary measure as public shorthand for the tongue, not a claim that every occurrence of three inches names speech.

Occurrences.Kwic: 三寸氣斷，一火洞然
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X70/X70n1403.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Tianru Weize (天如惟則禪師語錄): Tianru Weize is the exact headword speaker. In the, Tianru Weize owns the exact evidence clause after the complete case.

Senses.Explanation: This separate sense names three inches, not the three-inch tongue. Three inches is a measure whose object and dimension are supplied by its construction. In the Boatman's case, Chuanzi Decheng says, 'the line hangs a thousand feet, its intent in the deep pool; three inches from the hook, why do you not speak?' (垂絲千尺。意在深潭。離鉤三寸。子何不道。). Zhang Shangying's verse preserves the same distance from the hook. Fozhao Deguang uses the measure for thickness when he says Huangbo's facial skin remains three inches thick (面皮厚三寸). Tianru Weize's mortality warning applies the same small-span image to breath: 'when the three-inch breath is cut off, one fire burns through' (三寸氣斷，一火洞然). Distance, thickness, and the measured-breath image differ in what is measured, not in the lexical value of three inches; they therefore remain one sense rather than three context-driven senses.
